title: Cows live on grass, right?
hook: It aces the test photos. Has it learned what a cow looks like?

knows: that a model is trained on labelled examples and then tested
doesNotKnow: that a model can learn a cue that merely travels with the label
that test data from the same source can share the shortcut

misconception: If a model scores well on test data, it has learned the thing we meant.
objective: The learner can explain that a model takes whichever clue works best on its training data, so a high score proves the clue worked there, not that it is the intended clue; changing the conditions (here, shuffling backgrounds) exposes a shortcut.

claims.text: The toy has 20 invented training photos (10 cows, 10 camels). The background matches the label on 19 (95%); the shape clue, a visible hump meaning camel, is right on 16 (80%): 2 cows show a hump and 2 camels hide theirs.
claims.source: The lesson's own data in Demo.tsx (TRAIN); accuracy(TRAIN, "background") = 0.95 and accuracy(TRAIN, "shape") = 0.8 when run.

claims.text: The toy model uses one clue at a time and keeps the one with the higher training score: background.
On 20 test photos with backgrounds shuffled (half the cows on sand, half the camels on grass), the background clue is right on 10 of 20 (50%) and the shape clue still on 16 of 20 (80%).
claims.source: With backgrounds independent of the label and matching half the time, a background rule is right exactly when the background matches: 10 / 20. Reproduced by running accuracy(TEST, …) from Demo.tsx: 0.5 and 0.8.

claims.text: About real systems: image classifiers have been found to rely on backgrounds and other shortcuts that travel with the label in training data, and to fail when the background changes.
claims.source: Beery, Van Horn & Perona 2018, “Recognition in Terra Incognita”, ECCV (camera-trap classifiers fail at new locations); Geirhos et al. 2020, “Shortcut learning in deep neural networks”, Nature Machine Intelligence 2, 665–673 (discusses cows in unusual locations).

claims.text: A model takes the cheapest clue that works on its training data, and test photos drawn from the same source share the shortcut, so a high score there does not show the model learned the clue you meant.
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 2. Geirhos et al. 2020, Nature Machine Intelligence 2, 665-673 (shortcuts that work on i.i.d. test sets but fail out of distribution). 'Cheapest' is a loose paraphrase of simplicity/shortcut bias, not a measured quantity; the reviewer should confirm the wording is acceptable. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check.

recall.question: A model spots pneumonia on X-rays from Hospital 1 with 95% accuracy. Hospital 1 also stamps its scans differently when the patient is very ill. What should you test before trusting it?
options: X-rays from another hospital, without that stamp
Nothing: 95% on held-out scans is proof enough
recall.why: The model may be reading the stamp, a clue that travels with the label at Hospital 1. Only data where that shortcut is broken shows whether it learned the disease.
